name: Fiji
summary_text: Private adult consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful in Fiji since 1 February 2010, when the Crimes Decree 2009, cited as the Crimes Act 2010, took effect and repealed the historic Penal Code offence under Article 175. That offence had carried a maximum penalty of fourteen years imprisonment.  In April 2005 two men, Australian tourist Thomas McCosker and Fijian man Dhirendra Nadan, received two-year prison sentences under Article 175 for consensual sex. The trial judge described the acts as so disgusting that any decent person would vomit. Human Rights Watch called for the charges to be dropped and the men released, citing the 1997 constitutional prohibition on sexual orientation discrimination. The convictions were overturned in August 2005 by the highest court as a violation of the Constitution.  Enforcement ended in practice before repeal. In July 2006 the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested.  Fiji prohibited sexual orientation discrimination in its 1997 Constitution, the second such constitutional protection in the world after South Africa. That Constitution was abolished in 2009. The Constitution promulgated in September 2013 reinstated the protection and extended it. Article 26(3)(a) bans unfair direct or indirect discrimination on grounds including sex, gender, gender identity and expression and sexual orientation. In 2013 the Government also included sexual orientation and gender identity in anti-hate speech law and in law dealing with discrimination in certain businesses.  No legal route exists for a trans person to change a gender marker. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, despite the constitutional protection on gender identity and expression. A 2023 Asia Pacific Alliance policy brief and case study on legal gender recognition describes this as constitutional protection with zero implementation, resulting in documented marginalisation and discrimination.  Fiji recognises a traditional third-gender population known as vaka sa lewa lewa, people assigned male at birth who dress, act and behave as female. Sources describe this group as traditionally accepted by Fijian society. That acceptance has no legal effect.  Fiji provides no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions. The Marriage Act 2002 limits marriage to one man and one woman, with an express ban on same-sex marriage since 2002. Prime ministerial opposition was reaffirmed on 26 March 2013, in January 2016 and in 2019.  Lack of trust in police due to possible harassment likely discourages LGBTQ people from reporting anti-gay violence or hateful discrimination. Reports describe hate crimes as rare. Documented cases include the brutal murder in Suva on 1 July 2001 of Red Cross leader John Maurice Scott and his partner Gregory Scrivener in an apparent homophobic attack with a possible political motive, the brutal murder in Suva in May 2018 of a young transgender woman, and a gay student found dead in Nasinu in September 2017. Activists report that physical violence and domestic abuse operate as familial conversion therapy for many LGBTQ+ people.  Reports of societal discrimination and bullying are described as not uncommon. Social mores regarding sexual orientation and gender identity are described as conservative, with little public support for LGBTQ rights. Majority Methodist and Catholic denominations traditionally view transgender identities negatively. The Muslim minority, about 6% of the population, tends to view cross-dressing as sinful behavior that needs to be fixed. In April 2005 Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex and called homosexuality a sin in a conservative Christian nation, days after the two-year sentences noted above.  Public displays of affection are not illegal. Visitors are advised that such displays are generally considered offensive.  The Government has in the past cancelled gay pride marches. LGBTQ activists organised activities on 17 May 2013 for the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia, held an event in Suva in 2017 attended by activists and religious figures, and held Fiji's first pride parade on 17 May 2018 in Lautoka with local police escort and an address by former President Epeli Nailatikau.

name: Gabon
summary_text: Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is lawful in Gabon for men and women. No offence covering same-sex conduct is in force after the repeal completed in July 2020.  Gabon became independent in 1960 without inheriting a sodomy statute from the prior administration. Same-sex conduct was not an offence at any point before 2019.  Criminalisation was introduced by Law No. 042/2018, the new penal code that entered into force on 5 July 2019. Article 402 placed "les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe" within "atteintes aux mœurs" without using the term homosexuality. Conviction exposed a person to up to six months imprisonment and a fine of up to five million CFA francs, reported as about US$8,500 to US$8,561.  Enforcement followed within months. Two men were reported arrested under the 2019 provision and released only after paying bribes to police. Police had also arrested two men described as alleged gay spouses in December 2013 and released them.  Parliament removed the offence in mid-2020. The National Assembly approved decriminalisation on 23 June 2020, the Senate approved on 29 June, and presidential signature on 7 July 2020 restored the pre-2019 position that same-sex conduct is not criminal.  The age rules have changed over time. Historically the age of consent was unequal at 15 for opposite-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts. The 2020 repeal settlement set the age of sexual majority at 15 for girls and 18 for boys regardless of partner sex.  The constitution adopted by referendum on 16 November 2024 rejected demands to re-criminalise homosexuality and codified privacy protection in Article 18. Article 16 retains a marriage definition that excludes same-sex couples. That definition took effect on 12 April 2025 as a union between two people of opposite sex and is entrenched as unamendable. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition.  Gabon provides no legal gender recognition. It provides no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. The criminal provisions described in the sources concern same-sex sexual activity, not gender identity.  Police are reported to occasionally use "breaches of modesty" charges to target people with non-gender-conforming presentations and to target same-sex couples. Such discriminatory misuse of neutral laws is described as not widespread.  State-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is described as not present. Harassment by individuals is described as common, and societal discrimination was documented for the 2019 criminalisation year. Limited protection based on sexual orientation and sexual life exists under Law No. 025/2023 of 9 July 2023 amending Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011, which treats sexual orientation and sexual life as sensitive personal data.
